clue.text: Defeated criminal paid for 2 charges

parts.note: a con is a convict, the crossword's standard criminal

indicators.note: to charge is to rush straight at something, and a piece that rushes at a word ends up in the middle of it

parts.note: to fund something is to pay for it
2 down turns out to be NOTHING, and nothing written as a figure is O

explanation.walkthrough: A bare number in a clue is a cross-reference: it stands for whatever 2 down turns out to be, so that entry has to be solved before this one can be.
explanation.definitionFit: To confound someone is to thwart them completely — 'confound their politics' in the anthem is a wish to see the other side defeated.

clue.text: With a C but no L or E, Wordle could be CRUSH

definitions.note: a crush is a noun, a dense throng of people

parts.note: with a C means the letter C is added to the pool

indicators.note: says the letters could be arranged into another word, so they are shuffled
but no L or E means both those letters are taken away from the word

parts.note: the online word game, used here for its letters
the two letters named, L and E, neither of which may stay

explanation.surface: A Wordle player muses that, with C present and L and E ruled out, today's word could be CRUSH.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but no' strips L and E from WORDLE; add the C and 'could be' rearranges the five letters. The capitalised CRUSH looks like a Wordle guess but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A crush is a dense mass of people packed together, a synonym of a throng.

clue.text: FA never fine time-wasting, ultimately

parts.note: 'no' is the flat refusal that 'never' amounts to
a fine thread and a thin one are the same thickness

indicators.note: what happens ultimately happens at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is wanted

parts.note: the closing letter of time-wastinG

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all football — the FA, a fine, time-wasting by the corner flag — and not one of those senses is the one being used.
explanation.definitionFit: FA is short for sweet Fanny Adams, the polite form of a ruder phrase, and both amount to none of anything at all.

clue.text: Suffering upset stomach — fine wine can be like that

indicators.note: a stomach in that state has everything churning inside it, and letters churned about will not stay in the order they arrived

parts.note: 'fine' and 'okay' are the same shrug of approval

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'fine' as the wine's quality and the sentence makes sense; read it as 'okay' and it becomes four letters to shake up. That double duty is the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaky describes a wine that has taken vanilla and spice from the barrel it matured in — a tasting note, not a complaint.

clue.text: Ascending ladder, support youngster

indicators.note: in a down clue, ascending means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a ladder in tights is a run
a sling supports an injured arm

explanation.surface: Someone up a ladder steadies themselves while holding a child.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface ladder is something you climb; here it is the British name for a run in tights, and 'Ascending' only works because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursling is an infant being nursed, so a young child in someone's care.

clue.text: US officer training is never over houses

indicators.note: a thing turned over ends up facing the other way, so the run of letters has to be read from its far end back
to house something is to have it living inside you, and here one phrase has the answer lodged in it

parts.note: trai(ngisne)ver holds six consecutive letters, and they read the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Training is never over' is a sergeant's motto and a set of instructions at the same time, which is why nothing in it looks like wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is the lowest commissioned rank in the US Navy, the American opposite number to a Royal Navy sub-lieutenant.

clue.text: Fifty fish nets reserved

indicators.note: a net closes round whatever it catches, so the word doing the catching ends up wrapped about the other

parts.note: cod is the crossword's default fish
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish nets' is one space away from fishnets, and that near-miss is the misdirection: here the fish does the catching rather than being caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cold keeps their feelings back from you, which is what a reserved manner does — a temperature word doing social work.

clue.text: Huge public expressions of disappointment in speech

parts.note: news that is out is public knowledge

indicators.note: said rather than written, so what is wanted is a word that sounds identical and is spelt differently

parts.note: a sigh is the noise disappointment makes, and SIGHS spoken comes out on paper as SIZE

explanation.walkthrough: Two registers glued together: 'out' from the newsroom and sighs from the sofa. The clue reads as one long grumble and is really a charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Outsize clothing is cut beyond the standard range, so the word means larger than what normally fits — huge by the shop's measure.

clue.text: Coot, gripped by rude urge, not behaving in line with convention

indicators.note: to be gripped is to be held fast inside something, which is where the setter's own letter finishes up
letters that will not behave are letters that refuse to stay in the order they were given

parts.note: Coot is the setter of this puzzle, and a setter's word for himself is I
eight letters of fodder for the shake-up

explanation.walkthrough: Setters drop themselves into their own clues constantly, so a byline turning up mid-sentence is nearly always doing duty as the single letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: What is de rigueur is demanded by etiquette rather than by law — French for 'of strictness', borrowed for social obligations.

clue.text: Faceless oafs backing industrial action, mostly in suburbs

indicators.note: without a face means losing the front letter of the word

parts.note: oafs are louts

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the letters are read from the end
mostly means all but the last letter is kept

parts.note: a strike is industrial action by workers

explanation.surface: Anonymous thugs supporting a strike are mostly to be found in the suburbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faceless' takes the first letter from LOUTS; 'mostly' trims STRIKE to STRIK and 'backing' turns it to KIRTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Outskirts are the outer districts of a town, where the suburbs lie.

clue.text: Lecher perched alongside westbound track

parts.note: to have perched is to have sat

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway, a track

explanation.surface: A lecher sits beside a railway line heading west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'westbound' signals reversal only in an across entry, where west is right to left; RY is the standard abbreviation for railway.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth a satyr is a lustful woodland creature, so the word is used for a lustful man.

clue.text: Comedian who's missed bend cycling cracks chin?

indicators.note: something that cracks a thing breaks into it, so it goes inside

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the chin, to sock them

indicators.note: cycling moves a letter round from one end of the word to the other

parts.note: to bend is to lean

explanation.surface: Someone missing a bend while cycling crashes and cracks their chin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chin' is a verb here, British slang for punching someone on the jaw. Sean Lock, a British stand-up and panel-show regular, died in 2021, hence 'who's missed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sean Lock was a much-loved British comic whose death in 2021 left fans mourning him.

clue.text: Stage production of Aida short of an alto and soprano

indicators.note: a production of something puts it together in a new form, here reshuffling letters
short of an means lacking one of the letter

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for alto in choral music

explanation.surface: A staging of Verdi's opera Aida that lacks an alto and a soprano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage production' looks like one phrase, but Stage is the definition; removing an A from AIDA leaves AID, rearranged as DAI.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais is a raised platform for a speaker, so a stage in the sense of a platform.

clue.text: Jack Grealish's girl, maybe, supping wine in France, being patriotic

parts.note: the jack is the flag a ship flies at the bow, the Union Jack being the famous one

indicators.note: to sup is to take a drink in, and a word that takes another in holds it inside

parts.note: WAG is the tabloid label for a footballer's wife or girlfriend
vin is what wine is called there

explanation.walkthrough: Every name here is a decoy: the footballer is only present so that 'girl' can mean WAG, and 'Jack' is nautical rather than anybody's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Flag-waving is patriotism performed rather than felt — the bunting and cheering kind, and usually said with a hint of scorn.

clue.text: Component of blood pressure behind false start in court

parts.note: P is pressure in physics and on a weather chart
a train running behind is running late
a serve that clips the net is a let, and it has to be taken again

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface is medical and nothing in the answer is legal: 'court' is the tennis kind, and that swap is what the clue turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: A platelet is one of the cell fragments in blood that clump together to seal a wound, so the definition is plain biology.

clue.text: Urge to bed emoji?

parts.note: to egg someone on is to urge them
to bed a seedling out is to plant it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a suggestive text message, which is precisely the reputation the aubergine icon has — Coot lets the surface do the winking.
explanation.definitionFit: The aubergine icon on a phone keyboard goes by its American name, so the question mark admits this defines a picture by what it shows.

clue.text: Telephone call in space — somewhat elaborate

parts.note: an em is a printer's space, as wide as the type is tall
giving someone a bell is giving them a ring
-ish on the end of a word is how English says somewhat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' has to be heard as a verb rather than an adjective, and that switch is the hard step, because the surface offers the adjective first.
explanation.definitionFit: To embellish a story is to add decorative detail it never had, which is one of the things elaborate means when it is a verb.

clue.text: Tell stories, for example about sovereign

indicators.note: turned about, a piece faces the other way, and with two letters that simply swaps them

parts.note: for example is EG, turned about to read GE
to tell stories is to lie

explanation.walkthrough: EG for 'for example' is a workhorse abbreviation, and setters spin it round about as often as they use it the right way up.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is the lord to whom homage is owed, so 'sovereign' names him by feudal power rather than by a crown or a coin.

clue.text: Batsman could face this serious injury

definitions.meaning: this cricket delivery, bowled by a spinner, turns away from a right-handed batsman
the same two words read as plain English: a broken leg

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves smell of cricket, which is the trap — 'face' belongs to the batsman and 'serious injury' belongs to the hospital, not the game.
explanation.definitionFit: One reading is cricket, the ball that spins away from the bat; the other is the hospital kind, a snapped tibia.

clue.text: Suddenly mention glimpse of Lune going into Lancaster

indicators.note: going into means the letter is placed inside the other word

parts.note: Burt Lancaster, the American film actor

indicators.note: only a glimpse is seen, just the first letter of the word

parts.note: a river, giving its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone abruptly remarks on catching sight of the River Lune as it flows into Lancaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lune really does flow through the city of Lancaster, but here Lancaster is the actor Burt; 'going into' puts L inside BURT.
explanation.definitionFit: To blurt something is to say it suddenly and without thinking.

clue.text: Obscure type of weapon Greek character brought round

indicators.note: bringing the letters round turns them about, so the two letters swap order in place

parts.note: a nuclear weapon is one type
nu is the Greek letter N

explanation.surface: A shadowy sort of weapon is brought round by a Greek man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek character is not a person but a letter of the alphabet, and it is already sitting at the front of the weapon word, waiting to be turned about.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscure is hard to make out, so its meaning is not clear.

clue.text: Recent arrival discovered domes C Wren designed

indicators.note: the architect designed something new, so the letters are rearranged into a fresh plan
dis-covered means with the cover removed, so the outer letters of domes go

parts.note: the inside letters of domes are kept
taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Christopher Wren designed domes, and here they are being uncovered as a new discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' strips DOMES to OME; add C and WREN and 'designed' rearranges the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A newcomer is someone who has only lately arrived somewhere.

clue.text: Lunchbox cover located by staff

indicators.note: to be located by something is to sit right beside it, which is how these two halves join up

parts.note: to staff a desk is to man it
a hood covers an engine or a head

explanation.walkthrough: Definition and answer are both newspaper euphemisms, which is how the clue gets away with being this rude while reading like an office memo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunchbox is tabloid slang for the bulge in a sportsman's shorts, and manhood is the coy newspaper word for the same thing.

clue.text: Man of the cloth's endless compassion over late queen

indicators.note: in a down entry whatever is over sits above, so that piece is written first

parts.note: MERCY with no end to it is MERC
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen crosswords mean

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of the cloth' means a vicar almost everywhere else in English, and here it means a draper.
explanation.definitionFit: A mercer is a dealer in fine fabric, so the definition is meant with a straight face: the trade, not the clergy.

clue.text: Boldly race criminal in encounter close to home

indicators.note: a criminal has no respect for the order things are meant to be kept in, so the letters are free to move

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' reads as an adjective describing the racer and works as the instruction — the double duty setters like best.
explanation.definitionFit: A local derby is a match between two clubs from the same town, so both the rivalry and the short journey are in the phrase.

clue.text: Insult by sending cakes back

indicators.note: to send a thing is to set it travelling, and the direction it travels is what happens to the letters
this is an across entry, so going back means being read right to left along the row

parts.note: buns are the cakes on the tea trolley, and they travel backwards

explanation.walkthrough: Cakes are a crossword staple — buns, tarts, eccles — and for a four-letter answer the first of those is nearly always the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: To snub someone is to cut them dead in public, an insult delivered by withholding something rather than by saying anything.

clue.text: In bottom position? That makes Bert alert

parts.note: Bert turns into alert when its first letter is swapped for the pair A-L; the solution, split up, spells out that instruction

explanation.surface: A question about who is at the bottom, then a remark on how Bert becomes alert.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: split the solution into three short words and it reads as the instruction that turns Bert into alert. 'That makes' points from the solution to the change.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forming or lying at the base of a structure is in the bottom position.

clue.text: American leaves home for university party

indicators.note: someone who leaves is no longer there, so those letters walk out of the word they were in

parts.note: a campus is the grounds a university calls home
US is short for American, and it is the pair that walks out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' is the trap: nothing here is a celebration, and the word wanted is the one for a side in an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: A party in the sense of a faction — the Remain camp, the Corbyn camp — is a camp, so this is the political sense, not the birthday one.

clue.text: Disinclined to move from Gewürztraminer tasting

indicators.note: a helping taken from something is only part of what was there, and the part wanted is a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: the wanted letters run consecutively across the boundary between the two words, starting partway through the wine's name and finishing with the first letter of 'tasting'

explanation.walkthrough: A long foreign word is a gift to a hidden clue, because nobody reads it letter by letter — they are too busy trying to pronounce it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inert stays put and will not react: a chemist's inert gas does nothing at all, and a person described that way is just as immovable.

clue.text: Money's invested in those who produce furnaces

indicators.note: to invest originally meant to clothe, so money invested in a word is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: the people who make things are creators
M is money in the economists' M0 and M1, and crosswords borrow it

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a business story right up to the last word, and 'furnaces' is the giveaway: this is machinery, not investment.
explanation.definitionFit: A cremator is the furnace itself, the oven in a crematorium, so the definition names the machines and not the people who work them.

clue.text: Became aware of gathered mob

indicators.note: gathered, as in picked up by ear, signals the word is taken as it sounds

parts.note: heard means became aware of, learned

explanation.definitionFit: A herd is a large crowd of people, used disparagingly, so it is a synonym of mob.

clue.text: What can stop British playboy duke entering insane plea?

parts.note: a playboy is a rake

indicators.note: entering means the letter goes inside the other letters
an insane plea is a mad one, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A courtroom question: what could halt a British playboy duke who pleads insanity?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question rather than a noun: what can stop a car. The duke goes inside the jumbled plea, not after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake pedal is the control a driver presses to halt a car.
